name: Skarp laser razor

card.summary: A crowdfunded razor concept that promised to cut hair with laser light for a close, irritation-free shave; it has not reached the market.

quick.overview:
The Skarp laser razor was announced in 2015 by Skarp Technologies as a razor that used laser light to cut hair instead of a metal blade. The pitch was a cleaner shave with less irritation and no replacement blades.

For a man's looks the promise was smooth, even facial hair grooming without razor burn. The product itself has not been released, so there is no user experience to report.
quick.how: The company said the device would run on an AAA battery for about a month, be waterproof and be about the size of a disposable razor. It claimed to target chromophores in the hair shaft through an optical fiber, unlike laser hair removal, which targets follicles.[1]
quick.risks: Because the device never shipped, there is no safety record. Backers who paid into the campaigns faced financial risk: Kickstarter cancelled the 2015 campaign for lacking a working prototype, and Indiegogo backers had not received product years later.[1]

lead: The Skarp laser razor was a shaving device promoted by Skarp Technologies of Irvine, California, co-founded by Morgan Gustavsson and Paul Binun. It was presented in 2015 as 'The Skarp Laser Razor: 21st Century Shaving'.[1][2]

Its Kickstarter campaign asked for $160,000 and raised more than $4 million before Kickstarter cancelled it in October 2015, saying Skarp had not provided a working prototype as its rules require. CNET reported that the prototype cut only one or two hairs at a time. A new Indiegogo campaign raised over $500,000 and promised delivery in March 2016.[1]

The date was missed repeatedly; the last Indiegogo update was in March 2022 and, according to Wikipedia, no official release had occurred as of December 2025.[1] Hacker News commenters in 2015 questioned the video's tone and predicted delays.[2]

chain: Laser light cuts hair instead of a blade
angle.text: The claim was a close shave without razor burn or replacement blades. The device has not been released.

paras: Skarp launched on Kickstarter in September 2015, raised over $4 million, and had the campaign cancelled in October 2015. It relaunched on Indiegogo within hours.[1] Delivery promised for March 2016 slipped to the end of 2016 and later updates in 2018 and 2019 said it remained in development.[1] Gustavsson filed Chapter 7 bankruptcy in February 2023, and a lawsuit between the co-founders was reported in 2021.[1]

The company said the razor cut hair by targeting hair's chromophores through an optical fiber, rather than targeting follicles as laser hair removal does.[1] Reviewers questioned feasibility and the production timeline.[1]

timeline.event: Kickstarter campaign launched and cancelled; Indiegogo campaign begins.[1]
